`AgentDisplayState(owner, room, safe_activity, appearance_ref, display_revision).`

Do not store raw provider keys or full secrets as normal user-visible records. Raw media and 3D assets belong in appropriate file/object delivery storage; store references and permissions in the database. Keep source content and private rationale separate from the small shared projections.

Example solver contract: solve(snapshot\_ref, confirmed\_constraints, candidate\_set, committed\_component\_refs, fairness\_policy) → status, candidate\_set\_version, plans, private\_impacts, verification\_inputs, unresolved\_checks. No model-generated chat is required as a solver input.

Example publish contract: publish\_proposal(job\_id, attempt\_token, input\_revision, membership\_revision, permission\_revision, proposal\_terms, evidence\_refs, idempotency\_key). The server computes/verifies canonical terms digests; accepting a caller-supplied hash without the terms would not establish integrity.

Example frontend read contract: shared proposal terms \+ my allocation \+ my effective consent \+ current room revisions. It does not contain everybody's private caps. A hash binds data to a version; it does not prove the data is true or constitute a legally binding signature.

AgentMessage(envelope, body, utterance, thread\_id, effective\_audience, sanitization\_status, processing\_state);

ConversationThread(room, thread\_id, participant\_agent\_ids, topic\_ref, input\_revision, turn\_budget, state).

# **16\. Privacy, safety, and retention**

![][image10]

The promised boundary is controlled disclosure to other participants and scoped processing by necessary service/model providers. It is not anonymity, end-to-end encryption from the service, secure multiparty computation, or an inability to infer private preferences. Per-agent prompts are not security isolation.

Only give a model or tool the context required for that task. A trusted solver may need an exact cap; a public explanation model does not. Log source IDs and outcomes instead of sensitive stories. Disable or redact verbose hosted traces for real personal data. Developers viewing operational logs are part of the threat model.

Use scoped read/write paths, input validation, allowlisted tools/domains, request-size limits, safe URL handling, and outbound restrictions. Do not let a venue page, another agent's message, or a user prompt supply executable instructions to bypass permissions. No payment tools, arbitrary shell access, or unrestricted internal-network fetches are exposed.

Sharing is revocable for future access and processing. Revocation cannot erase what a person already read or recorded. Invalidate pending summaries and cached retrieval outputs; exclude revoked records on every new read. Remove them from active checkpoints or restart affected threads. Define backup/provider retention before promising deletion. Current behavior and retention duration must be visible, not implied.

Private reasons are optional. Do not collect medical detail when a simple accommodation requirement is sufficient. Do not infer social anxiety diagnoses, personality disorders, financial hardship, or relationship quality. Ask what the person wants the app to do, not why they deserve a boundary.

The PRD asks to show who is reviewing and to avoid public pressure. These can conflict. Proposed safer default: neutral shared pending status and private reminders. Named review status needs an explicit team/product decision. This architecture flags the conflict rather than silently changing PRD §8.

No interface can technically guarantee freedom from interpersonal pressure. Provide equally usable decline controls, no countdown penalties, no shaming character animations, and a way to leave or pause. Measure whether people felt heard; do not optimize for the highest approval rate regardless of how it was obtained.

# **17\. Frontend, characters, live progress, and offline behavior**

Next.js renders My Agent, Consensus Journey, Live Negotiation, Group Agreement, and Options as specified in the PRD. Maintain the private/shared distinction in information layout, URL handling, browser caching, notifications, and screenshots shown during a demo.

Next.js renders My Agent, Consensus Journey, Live Negotiation, Group Agreement, and Options as specified in the PRD. Live Negotiation shows real Apify initial-search and targeted-research milestones with source labels and timestamps. Maintain the private/shared distinction in layout, URLs, caching, notifications, and screenshots; never expose private search criteria or Actor credentials.

Store semantic character state and customization, not every animation frame. Render movement, blinking, and transitions locally. Mark work as paused when the worker is paused. Characters must not celebrate a person's consent before it exists or look disappointed when someone declines. Provide reduced-motion and ordinary keyboard-accessible controls outside the 3D canvas.

On refresh, resubscribe and wait for an applied authoritative snapshot before enabling approvals. A cached plan can be displayed as stale/read-only while disconnected. Permit local drafts if useful, but do not queue an offline acceptance to silently apply to changed terms. On reconnect, reconcile versions and ask for review when needed.

Multiple tabs belong to one human identity. They do not create additional votes. Multiple concurrent decisions from that identity use version checks and idempotency. Log-out and account-switch flows clear private caches and subscriptions. Never show the previous account's pending private card while a new account loads.

An offline member's authorized agent may research within previously confirmed boundaries. Missing information waits; final human approval stays pending. Returning users get a safe recap and the current proposal, not a replay of provider calls. Replay is a visual reading of retained permitted events, not re-execution.

Voice is optional. Audio transport and transcription are separate from state synchronization. Confirm interpreted constraints and keep text fallback. Store only necessary approved transcripts; do not auto-play confidential speech in the shared room.

# **18\. Deployment, scaling, performance, and observability**

MVP deployment: one Next.js deployment, one pinned SpacetimeDB module/database, one always-on Python worker with persistent checkpoint storage, and a lightweight long-lived TypeScript subscription dispatcher (which can share the worker host). Keep vendor credentials server-side. Do not depend on a short-lived serverless request handler to maintain the dispatcher subscription. No Kubernetes, dedicated agent server per person, or separate message broker is required.

MVP deployment: one Next.js deployment, one SpacetimeDB database/module, one always-on Python worker with LangGraph and the Apify Research Gateway, and a lightweight long-lived TypeScript subscription dispatcher (which can share the worker host). Apify credentials and Actor configuration remain server-side. Keep a deterministic fixture mode and one tested flight Actor; add a stay Actor after its output passes validation. No Kubernetes, separate agent server per person, or separate message broker is required.

SpacetimeDB is both the durable application queue and the reactive change source for this bounded build, not a replacement for every specialized broker at arbitrary scale. The preferred path is a worker-authorized TypeScript subscription dispatcher that wakes Python when eligible jobs change. On startup, reconnect, or missed notifications, scan indexed outstanding jobs; keep bounded periodic reconciliation as a safety net. All workers still claim jobs transactionally with leases and fencing tokens. Measure the design before scaling or adding another queue.

N participants are supported in the data model, but performance must be tested. Flight discovery can fan out across origins and date windows: bound Apify concurrency, total Actor runs, result counts, rate/cost budgets, and candidate-set size; cache permitted results with timestamps and freshness rules. Deduplicate research and prune unsuitable candidates before solving. Agent negotiation and human wait time remain separate bottlenecks.

Optimization changes should reuse safe unchanged candidates and previous feasible solutions where appropriate. Do not promise millisecond end-to-end negotiation; model calls, external research, human response, and solver difficulty vary. Separate time spent computing from time waiting for people.

Measure time to initial Apify results, Actor failure/empty-result rate, completeness and freshness, price/route normalization accuracy, initial versus targeted candidate counts, solver feasibility changes, research spend, and user-change-to-proposal latency. Also track dispatch, solve/validation, stale rejection, retries, and model/tool cost. Record tested Actor versions and data modes; do not claim live inventory without evidence.

Set per-room spending limits for infrastructure calls and bounded retries with backoff. Budget exhaustion pauses the job visibly. Do not switch models or synthetic data silently. A documented fallback can retain functionality, but outputs must identify limitations.

# **19\. Edge-case register and required handling**

This register defines expected behavior to implement and test. It does not claim the tests have passed or that every possible failure has been eliminated. Authorization, hard-constraint, consent, and stale-result failures block claims that the corresponding protection works.

**E01 — Ambiguous budget or date.** Ask a targeted question; preserve the original text and tentative extraction. Do not assume currency, date, timezone, cap strength, or scope. Test “around 500” and “home Monday.”

**E02 — Same value, different meaning.** A hard cap and a flexible target produce different eligible options and consultation behavior. Test that the hard cap is never exceeded and the soft range is not treated as final acceptance.

**E03 — Conflicting profile and session inputs.** Show the conflict privately; require confirmation of the scoped exception. Do not overwrite persistent preferences from one trip decision.

**E04 — User will not explain a reason.** Accept the boundary without explanation. Continue only within known permissions; do not infer a motive or repeatedly demand it.

**E05 — User says no without a replacement plan.** Keep the proposal unagreed and offer a bounded clarification or pause. Do not require the person to supply the solution.

**E06 — Only one valid candidate.** Present one with its limitations; do not fabricate an alternative. Distinguish this from a true blocker.

**E07 — No candidate satisfies all requirements. Distinguish 'no feasible combination in current Apify/fixture candidates' from global impossibility. Run a bounded, permissioned targeted Apify re-search if useful; otherwise explain coverage and ask whether to broaden criteria. Never relax a hard limit silently.**

**E08 — Solver timeout or invalid model.** UNKNOWN remains unresolved; MODEL\_INVALID is an engineering error. Retain a separately verified incumbent only with accurate status. Never label either as proven global infeasibility.

**E09 — Missing amenity, capacity, or accessibility evidence.** Keep unknown values explicit; block a claim of complete verification where they are critical. Published advertising is not guaranteed fulfillment.

**E10 — Currency, tax, fee, or timezone mismatch.** Normalize units and include known mandatory charges; reject incomplete totals when a hard budget depends on them. Preserve local travel times and date boundaries in the UI.

**E11 — Hotel nights, shared costs, or transport double-counted.** Validate occupancy, date ranges, per-unit versus total price, and allocation. Test totals independently of the solver's score.

**E12 — Flight/room availability is stale or unverified. An Apify-observed listing is not confirmed inventory. Refresh observations or cross-check with an authoritative provider if available; label uncertainty and reopen relevant review when critical facts expire or change. Do not assume separately discovered offers can all be booked for the party.**

**E13 — Previously approved quote expires.** Preserve historical acceptance but mark current offer validity stale. Recheck or replan; changed material terms require fresh acceptance.

**E14 — Participant reports an existing external booking.** Treat it as a user-reported commitment with its source/verification status. Keep it fixed unless they authorize exploring a change; never cancel or claim payment verification.

**E15 — Agent wants to exceed an exploration allowance.** Block the proposed action in code and ask the owner. A tool field such as requires\_approval=false cannot override policy.

**E16 — Agent generates an invented concession or source.** Reject unsupported values and references; fall back to a question or known candidate. Test that fluent text cannot create a valid option.

**E17 — Duplicate or reordered agent messages.** Deduplicate by stable ID and process only matching round/revision; buffer or reject inconsistent messages. A duplicate counteroffer cannot create a second approval or repeated user prompt.

**E18 — Unknown message schema or oversized payload.** Reject with a safe error and no state mutation. Do not interpret malformed content as consent or execute arbitrary suggested tools.

**E19 — Agent crashes, loops, or never answers.** Preserve completed evidence, retry within budget, then pause with a clear reason. An unresponsive agent is not an accepting participant.

**E20 — Two participants change requirements simultaneously.** Commit both confirmed changes with revision checks; reschedule against a coherent latest snapshot. If one person's edit conflicts with their own stale edit, ask them to reconcile.

**E21 — Old solver result finishes last.** Reject its current-publication attempt; mark superseded. Do not let completion time determine which plan is authoritative.

**E22 — Worker lease expires during an external call.** A replacement attempt gets a new token; old publication is fenced off. Record possible duplicate provider cost honestly.

**E23 — Database commit succeeds but response is lost.** Retry the same idempotency key and read the existing result. A new key is not the default retry strategy.

**E24 — Graph restarts around a human interrupt.** Reread current question/revision/permission state; do not resend the same question or apply a stale answer. Protect operational checkpoints as private data.

**E25 — Three accept, one declines or is pending.** Remain unagreed. Do not advance the shared milestone or announce consensus.

**E26 — Stale tab submits approval.** Reject terms/revision mismatch and show the latest review card. A positive button click cannot authorize an unseen replacement.

**E27 — A person withdraws after approval.** Invalidate their effective consent for the relevant agreement, reopen review, and stop dependent progression. This is not an automatic booking cancellation.

**E28 — Approval and withdrawal race.** Transaction order governs; a later valid withdrawal reopens the agreement. Recompute derived milestones rather than keeping a cached all-approved flag.

**E29 — User, agent, or organizer tries to approve for someone else.** Reject using authenticated identity and operation role. Agent evaluation is never converted to human consent.

**E30 — Member offline or browser closes.** Save pending state; allow only authorized research; offer optional private reminders. On return show current state and a permitted recap, not a reset or assumed acceptance.

**E31 — Member joins, leaves, or invitation is reused.** Verify the invitation and membership change, revise group terms and affected sets, revoke future access as needed, and reevaluate shared prices. Do not treat a smaller group as original-group consensus.

**E32 — A previously unaffected component turns out to share a budget or dependency.** Reopen all affected components and explain the relation. When the dependency graph is incomplete, conservatively expand review.

**E33 — Privacy permission is revoked mid-generation.** Cancel or suppress the output, recheck permission at delivery, and rebuild from permitted data. Revocation cannot retract knowledge already seen.

**E34 — Shared text, totals, timing, or named review state reveals private information.** Reduce detail, use safe templates, and test actual payloads. State that inference cannot be fully prevented; do not claim anonymous negotiation.

**E35 — Another account requests a private table/view or room.** Deny before retrieval and before model context construction. Test direct API access as well as the visible interface.

**E36 — Account switch leaves old data cached.** Clear subscriptions/caches and require a fresh authorized snapshot. Private previews must not survive into the new account.

**E37 — A source page or incoming message contains prompt injection.** Treat it as data, deny unauthorized tool actions, and keep secret/approval paths unavailable. Run adversarial fixtures against the gateway.

**E38 — Apify Actor returns rate limits, empty/partial results, an anti-bot block, or timeout. Use bounded backoff and stored run IDs, show incomplete coverage, and offer clearly labeled cached/fixture fallback. Never invent current prices or call a scraped listing 'bookable'.**

**E39 — Apify Actor schema changes, duplicates a listing, or omits fare/fee fields. Validate per-Actor contracts, quarantine bad records, deduplicate flight identities and source URLs, and avoid double-counting costs, options, or capacity. Missing critical fields remain unknown rather than zero.**

**E40 — No measurable progress or recurring disagreement.** Pause after the configured budget. Ask a useful optional question or accept no agreement; do not use repetition to wear someone down.

**E41 — Suggested cost split burdens one person disproportionately.** Show private impacts and allowed shared facts; require explicit permission for new liability. No fairness score can override refusal.

**E42 — Infrastructure or network outage.** Disable consequential actions until current state is known, retain durable work, expose offline/stale status, and recover from persisted jobs. Do not present a local animation as a committed decision.

**E43 — A schema/module deployment interrupts an active room.** Use a compatible migration, regenerate clients, test upgrade fixtures, and preserve old immutable proposal interpretation. Version payloads and decline unsupported transitions safely.

**E44 — User deletes a profile or memory.** Remove active retrieval paths, stop scoped jobs, invalidate derived outputs where required, and apply the documented retention policy to checkpoints/logs/backups. Preserve only justified minimal audit information; do not promise instantaneous erasure everywhere.

**E45 — Group size exceeds tested limits.** Reject or queue gracefully using a configured maximum, not a hardcoded four-agent assumption. Explain the tested limit and performance status.

**E46 — User asks for booking, payments, or points transfer.** Explain that this MVP provides planning and handoff only. No transaction tools are available; agreement must not be relabeled as reservation.

E47 — An utterance reveals private information. Block delivery, regenerate from the room-voice context, or fall back to a template. Test with adversarial fixtures containing private caps and reasons.

E48 — An utterance contradicts or exceeds its typed payload. Reject and regenerate; text never overrides the typed act.

E49 — Agents loop in polite back-and-forth. Close the thread on the turn budget or when no new act or evidence appears; escalate to the mediator or a human question.

# **20\. Testing, PRD traceability, and measurable claims**

Unit tests cover Actor-specific adapters, route/date/timezone/currency normalization, missing fare/tax fields, deduplication, freshness, provenance, permission checks, deterministic constraints, hashing, and state transitions. Integration tests cover initial Apify discovery, a conflict-driven targeted Actor run that changes candidates, worker claims, typed messages, graph pause/resume, publication, and fixture fallback. Playwright uses separate authenticated browser contexts.

Property/invariant tests should generate changing inputs, responses, memberships, and retry orderings. After each operation, assert that no current agreed proposal violates confirmed modeled hard constraints; no missing required acceptance appears as agreement; no old job overwrites a newer generation; and unauthorized identities receive no raw private fields.

PRD US01–US02 map to confirmed extraction and hard/flexible clarification; US03/US09 to privacy; US04 to distinct scoped agents; US05–US06 to Apify-sourced candidates, actual re-search, and validation; US07/US10 to consent; US08 to concession permission; US11 to replanning; US12 to versioned records; US13 to a live judge-entered change. Test that the first research call precedes initial optimization and that targeted research can alter feasible options.

Compare three internal versions on the same candidate fixtures, constraints, model family where applicable, and disclosure rules: A, one LLM proposes; B, one LLM plus the same solver and consent safeguards; C, our personal agents, mediator, solver, and consent safeguards. Keep security controls equal where they are not the variable under test. Otherwise a better result could come from the solver or UI rather than the agent architecture.

Measure hard violations, valid options, worst and total declared burden, user interventions, unaffected agreements retained, clarification quality, unsupported claims, latency, retries, and cost. Report dataset size, settings, failures, and user-study limits. Privacy and approval checks are release gates, not claims of a universal guarantee after a few tests.

Do not optimize for speed to yes alone. Record unresolved disagreements and voluntary declines as valid outcomes. Optional post-review feedback asks whether the person understood the compromise, felt free to refuse, and felt represented. This does not establish reduced social anxiety or long-term relationship benefit.

ASI:One comparisons require comparable actual tests and disclosure of access/data differences. Public feature descriptions cannot establish missing competitor mechanisms. Internal benchmarks can validate our implementation without claiming market-wide superiority.

Extend US02: two users with the same confirmed budget and hardness but different participation preferences receive different objection routing, consultation timing, and reminder behavior.

Test that agent B's reply in a thread changes research, validation, or the selected proposal; that room utterances never contain private caps or reasons; and that utterance/payload mismatches are rejected.

# **21\. Build order, delivery, and sponsor boundaries**

**Milestone A** — Agree on identity, constraints, message envelopes, revisions, permissions, and proposal terms. Implement create/join room, isolated private views, shared subscriptions, one immutable proposal, and real human approvals without AI. This proves the application rules before model behavior complicates debugging.

**Milestone B — Connect labeled fixtures, CP-SAT, independent validation, worker leases, and version-checked publication. Add the small TypeScript subscription dispatcher and a startup/reconnect reconciliation scan so new durable jobs wake Python reactively, with polling only as fallback. A private requirement change must produce a genuinely different feasible result, while old approvals and late solver results are rejected.**

**Milestone C — Add Claude's proposed extraction and confirmation, typed personal-agent protocol, LangGraph pause/resume, and an Apify flight Actor adapter for INITIAL discovery. Verify Actor input/output, persist run/dataset IDs, normalize results, and keep a fixture fallback. Show that different owners' inputs lead to different agent evaluations.**

**Milestone D — Add targeted Apify re-search triggered by an actual agent objection/solver blocker; verify new candidates affect the solver, preserve provenance and private/shared evidence, and test reconnect, offline pending decisions, and important failures. Integrate a second stay/venue Actor only if its schema and results are reliable.**

**Milestone E** — Refine characters, collective progression, accessible controls, and the demonstration. Preserve a reproducible dynamic-fixture mode and clearly identify live data. Test an unexpected judge-entered change; do not present a prerecorded answer as live negotiation.

Suggested ownership follows the earlier discussion rather than creating new assignments: Ronit—constraint model, fairness policy, validator, and replanning; Skylar—agent protocol and orchestration; Elena—product flow, customer evidence, acceptance tests, and demo narrative; Anna—characters, frontend, and client integration. Explicitly agree who owns the SpacetimeDB module and cross-stack authorization. These cannot remain unassigned integration tasks.

The demonstration follows the PRD: different confirmed meanings behind similar budgets; an initial Apify flight search (or clearly labeled fixture fallback); real agent exchange; validated alternatives; private clarification; human acceptance; collective progression; a judge-entered change that triggers targeted Apify re-search; revised impacts; and renewed approvals. Show Actor source and timestamp without claiming scraped listings are booked inventory.

Sponsor evidence comes from the same working experience. SpacetimeDB: transactional consent, subscription-driven jobs, synchronized private/shared negotiation, stale-result rejection, recovery. Microsoft: a useful customer workflow with responsible controls. Meta: people heard and choosing together. Apify: initial real-world flight discovery AND targeted research that materially changes candidate sets and feasible compromises. No prize eligibility or performance is assumed without verification.

Fetch.ai is removed from the runtime and is not a target based on this implementation. CREAO remains optional; pursuing its supplied brief requires a genuinely core agent run and the specified submission evidence. Figma, voice, and other tracks require actual qualifying use. Do not add decorative integrations or duplicate orchestration just to list sponsors.

# **22\. Questions and answers**

## Q1. Why not put everything inside SpacetimeDB?

It is our primary backend. Ordinary application writes, authorization, agreement state, and live subscriptions belong there. Python remains a specialized worker because our agent and solver libraries run there. One authoritative backend does not require one runtime for every computation.

## Q2. Why is FastAPI optional now?

Reducers and views replace routine profile, room, proposal, and approval endpoints. Add a small HTTP service only for a concrete callback, webhook, or streaming requirement. That service uses the same authoritative operations rather than maintaining a parallel plan state.

## Q3. Does removing Fetch.ai remove real agent-to-agent communication?

No. We own the logical agent identities, typed envelopes, inboxes, delivery records, evaluations, and replies. Another agent genuinely receives and acts on a request using its own authorized context. We remove a provider/framework, not the behavior.

## Q4. Do we need one model or server per person?

No. Several logical agents can use the same model endpoint and worker infrastructure. Separate context, permissions, state, and responsibilities distinguish them. One website serves many browser sessions; four is the demo size, not a hardcoded platform limit.

## Q5. What does LangGraph do that SpacetimeDB does not?

LangGraph runs and resumes Python computation, including model calls, research, and human-input pauses. SpacetimeDB records authorized application state and decisions. The separation avoids rebuilding workflow support and prevents model execution from becoming the authority for consent.

## Q6. Why keep checkpoints outside the main database?

A checkpoint records where execution paused, not what the group currently agreed to. The proposed single-worker deployment uses a supported persistent checkpointer and reconciles it with SpacetimeDB on resume. A custom checkpointer is unnecessary unless a concrete requirement justifies building and testing one.

## Q7. Could one LLM plus a solver do the same task?

Possibly for some scenarios. Personal agents provide scoped context and continuing representation, but their extra coordination must earn its cost. Compare a single-agent-plus-solver baseline under the same constraints, candidates, permissions, and consent rules. Multiple agents alone do not prove better outcomes.

## Q8. What does Claude add beyond a form?

It can interpret incomplete requests, clarify ambiguity, ask optional reason-aware questions, propose allowed alternatives, and explain checked tradeoffs. A form remains a confirmation surface and fallback. Claude does not own permissions, arithmetic validity, or human approval.

## Q9. What exactly does Apify replace?

Apify replaces selected custom travel-data collection for both INITIAL flight discovery and TARGETED conflict-driven research. A tested Google Flights Actor is the primary flight listing source; additional stay/venue Actors are separate tested adapters. Apify does not guarantee seat inventory or replace the solver, mediator, consent, or authoritative booking verification. Duffel or another direct API is optional.

## Q10. Can the mediator see everyone's private conversation?

Not by design. Its language-model context receives shared or explicitly permitted facts. Trusted computation can separately process the minimum numeric constraints needed for validation. This is controlled processing inside our service, not secrecy from every service operator or model provider.

## Q11. Can a participant say no privately?

Yes: objections and reasons use owner-scoped paths, while the group receives only authorized summaries. But timing, totals, or changing options can still reveal clues. Do not promise anonymous negotiation, and avoid publicly identifying a holdout by default.

## Q12. What happens when someone never responds?

Their decision remains pending. Agents may continue authorized research, but the group cannot claim their agreement. Offer an opted-in private reminder or pause. Continuing with a smaller group requires an explicit membership change and a visibly new decision, not silently treating absence as yes.

## Q13. Why not let agents approve low-risk plans?

The PRD requires people to accept the affected terms. Agents may research and propose within permission without asking at every step. Final agreement is a separate authority. Delegated approval, spending, and automatic booking are outside this version.

## Q14. Can an agent negotiate a hard budget upward?

It cannot change the cap or treat an over-budget plan as valid. It can report that current candidates do not work and provide a non-pressuring clarification path. Only a new explicit owner confirmation changes the hard requirement.

## Q15. Does the fairness score tell us who is happiest?

No. It evaluates a declared modeling policy using known preference impacts. Show practical cost and time consequences, document weights and normalization, and let people disagree. A mathematically preferred result is not psychological consensus.

## Q16. Is a feasible plan guaranteed to be bookable?

No. It is feasible under encoded requirements and checked evidence. Inventory and prices can change, and sandbox or fixture data do not establish live availability. Recheck before handoff and keep approved, booked, and completed states separate.

## Q17. What if people approve different alternatives?

Their approvals remain attached to different proposal IDs and terms. They cannot be combined into consent for either option. The mediator can ask which alternative should be reviewed, but cannot merge incompatible votes into agreement.

## Q18. What if someone changes their mind after everyone approved?

Preserve the historical record, make that person's relevant acceptance ineffective, and reopen dependent review. Prior approval does not remove the ability to reconsider. An external booking remains an external commitment; the application does not silently cancel it.

## Q19. What if somebody joins while a summary is being generated?

Membership and audience revisions change. Suppress or rebuild pending output against current permissions, reassess shared costs and affected participants, and request the necessary reviews. New members do not automatically receive previously private or restricted material.

Q20. Can we show the agents' conversation?

Yes. The room conversation is designed to be shown live: each utterance is phrased from room-permitted facts only and sanitized before delivery. Exchanges about one owner's private terms appear only in that owner's My Agent view. The UI shows what agents said to each other, not the model's hidden chain-of-thought.

## Q21. What happens if a browser or worker crashes?

The browser reloads its authorized current snapshot. The worker reconciles durable jobs and execution checkpoints, uses stable operation keys, and resumes or restarts eligible work. Pending people stay pending. An obsolete attempt cannot overwrite current state.

## Q22. Can we guarantee exactly-once execution?

Not across external model and provider APIs. We use at-least-once delivery, deduplication, idempotent application effects, and provider idempotency where available. Some crashes can still cause duplicate external calls and cost; document that limit.

## Q23. How can unchanged approvals survive a new global revision?

The new revision invalidates obsolete computing jobs. A component's original approval can remain attached to the same immutable terms only after dependencies, audience, affected people, and validity are rechecked. Do not copy approval onto new terms. A changed complete package still needs the relevant final-plan review.

## Q24. Why validate again after the solver?

A solver can be correct for an incorrectly built model. Separate checks catch missing costs, stale evidence, incomplete participant coverage, or output conversion mistakes. They provide defense against errors, not a guarantee that every external fact is true.

## Q25. Can agents learn from previous trips?

They can reuse reviewable, scoped preferences the person confirms and chooses to retain. One compromise is not a permanent trait. We do not claim self-training or automatic improvement without an evaluated learning mechanism.

## Q26. Does a custom protocol make us different from ASI:One?

It makes the implementation independent. Product differentiation must come from tested interaction and behavior. Do not claim a competitor lacks a mechanism because public documentation does not explain its internals.

## Q27. How many people can the architecture support?

The schema supports variable membership. The demo tests four. A deployed limit must be configured and measured; more users increase search, model cost, coordination, and human response time. N is a design parameter, not an unlimited-scaling claim.

## Q28. How should we evaluate another proposed feature?

Check whether it strengthens the complete P0 experience and whether it changes privacy, state, permissions, candidate evidence, or consent contracts. Record the decision and version affected interfaces before adding a provider or parallel subsystem.

# **23\. Open decisions and sign-off checklist**

Still to confirm: login/identity recovery; Claude model/API access; exact Apify flight Actor and its tested input/output, terms, runtime, price completeness, run budget, and reliability; suitable stay Actor (the listed Agoda Actor is reviews only); optional provider cross-check; checkpoint deployment; tested group size; negotiation/research budgets; fairness weights; retention; pending-status visibility; affected-party rules; migrations/recovery; and owners for SpacetimeDB, dispatcher, and research gateway.

The separate optimisation strategy tab was empty when inspected for this update. The fairness objective here is a proposed implementation default, not an approved or implemented strategy from that tab. Resolve it against the PRD's open decision before claiming measured fairness.

The PRD requests at least two feasible tradeoffs or a true blocker. Exactly one feasible candidate is also a possible valid outcome. Discuss that wording with the team; never create a fake alternative to satisfy it. Likewise, neutral pending status is a proposed response to the tension between visibility and avoiding social pressure, not a silent rewrite of the PRD.

Before parallel implementation, agree on typed constraints, the message envelope, visibility rules, immutable proposal terms, exact consent semantics, and the input snapshot. Before the demo, verify isolated identities, private reads, a real counterproposal, a real replan, stale-write rejection, refusal/pending behavior, source labels, and end-to-end recovery.

Historical brainstorming and earlier diagrams may mention Fetch.ai or Duffel-first discovery. The authoritative current implementation is this ARCHITECTURE tab, the updated PRD, the updated Mermaid diagrams, and the Detailed TL;DR. The PRD remains product authority; unresolved policy choices still need explicit team sign-off.
